reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A disorder of the pilosebaceous unit affecting the face, chest, and back, typically beginning around puberty
The hallmark non-inflammatory lesion is the comedo (open blackheads and closed whiteheads); its presence distinguishes acne from other papulopustular eruptions like rosacea
Inflammatory lesions range from papules and pustules to deep nodules and cysts, and severe forms lead to scarring and post-inflammatory pigmentation
Treatment is chosen by severity: topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide for comedonal and mild inflammatory disease, adding topical or oral antibacterials for moderate disease
Combining benzoyl peroxide with antibacterials reduces bacterial resistance, and antibacterials should not be used as prolonged monotherapy
Systemic retinoid therapy is reserved for severe, nodulocystic, or scarring acne resistant to other measures and requires careful monitoring and strict pregnancy precautions given teratogenicity
Hormonal therapy can help women with acne linked to androgen excess; consider investigating for hyperandrogenism when there are virilising features or menstrual irregularity
Sudden severe nodular acne with fever and joint pain (acne fulminans) is a systemic emergency needing urgent specialist care
reference.pathophysiology: Acne results from four interacting processes within the pilosebaceous unit: increased sebum production driven by androgens, abnormal keratinisation of the follicular lining producing microcomedones, proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation. Trapped sebum and keratin form comedones; bacterial activity and the host immune response generate inflammatory mediators that produce papules, pustules, and deeper nodules. Rupture of the follicular wall extends inflammation into the dermis, and disordered wound healing can result in atrophic or hypertrophic scarring. Hormonal influences, genetic predisposition, and certain drugs modulate severity.
additionalDifferentials: Rosacea (lacks comedones, features flushing and telangiectasia)
Hidradenitis suppurativa when lesions involve flexures
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis; investigations rarely needed for typical presentations
Hormonal workup (androgens, and related endocrine tests) when hyperandrogenism or polycystic ovary syndrome is suspected
Pregnancy testing and lipid and liver monitoring before and during systemic retinoid therapy
Swabs when Gram-negative folliculitis or resistant infection is suspected
redFlags: Acne fulminans: abrupt severe ulcerating nodular acne with fever, malaise, and arthralgia
Signs of underlying endocrine disorder such as virilisation or rapid-onset severe acne
Extensive scarring or psychological distress requiring escalation of care
Suspected retinoid-associated mood disturbance during systemic treatment
reference.prognosis: Acne usually improves after adolescence but may persist into adulthood, particularly in women; early effective treatment limits permanent scarring and psychosocial impact.
pitfalls: Prolonged antibacterial monotherapy promoting resistance and relapse
Under-treating scarring or nodular acne and delaying referral for systemic retinoid therapy
Overlooking the significant psychological burden and risk of low mood
Failing to enforce pregnancy prevention during teratogenic systemic retinoid use
management: Topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide as first-line treatment for comedonal and mild inflammatory acne

Add a topical or oral antibacterial such as a tetracycline for moderate inflammatory disease, always combined with benzoyl peroxide and never used as prolonged monotherapy, to limit bacterial resistance
Hormonal therapy with a combined oral contraceptive or an anti-androgen such as spironolactone in appropriate women
Oral isotretinoin for severe, nodulocystic or scarring acne resistant to other measures, with monitoring and strict pregnancy-prevention measures given its teratogenicity
General measures with adherence support, non-comedogenic skin care and avoidance of aggravating factors
Treat and prevent sequelae such as scarring and post-inflammatory pigmentation and address the psychosocial impact
Dermatology referral for severe, scarring or treatment-resistant disease
